title: Reading Revelation

objectives.can: Read Revelation and notice where its Greek departs from the ordinary rules of agreement.

explanation.summary: Most of Revelation is ordinary New Testament Greek, joined by καί and rich in images. A few of its sentences, however, break the usual rules of case and agreement, and grammarians have long pointed them out. This lesson shows how to spot them, describes the explanations that have been proposed, and lets you read the passage with both in view.

sections.heading: Ordinary Greek most of the time
body: Look first at the regular parts. Revelation 21:1 reads καὶ εἶδον οὐρανὸν καινὸν καὶ γῆν καινήν: the verb εἶδον, 'I saw', then two objects in the accusative, each with its adjective agreeing with it. In 21:2 καταβαίνουσαν is accusative feminine singular and agrees with τὴν πόλιν. In 21:3, ἤκουσα φωνῆς μεγάλης … λεγούσης has the genitive after ἀκούω, and the participle λεγούσης agrees with φωνῆς.
The narrative runs on by καί, one clause after another, and the visionary calls attention with Ἰδού (1:7, 21:3, 21:5). If you have read John or Mark, the rhythm will be familiar.

sections.heading: Where the usual agreement is broken
body: The best-known case is Revelation 1:4. The preposition ἀπό normally takes the genitive, but the title that follows it is ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος. The article ὁ is nominative, and the phrase includes a finite verb, ἦν, which cannot have a case at all. In 1:8 the same title stands in its ordinary place: λέγει κύριος, ὁ θεός, ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος, where the nominative is correct because it describes the subject. In 1:4, after ἀπό, grammarians describe the nominative as a departure from the rule.

A second case follows in 1:5: καὶ ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός. Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ is genitive after ἀπό, but the words that explain it, ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός, ὁ πρωτότοκος … καὶ ὁ ἄρχων, are nominative. A noun in apposition would normally take the same case as the noun it explains.

A third is in 1:10–11. The voice is φωνὴν μεγάλην, accusative, but the participle that goes with it, λεγούσης, is genitive. Compare 21:3, where φωνῆς and λεγούσης agree. Such mismatches are scattered through the book; most of it is regular.

sections.heading: What has been proposed
body: Scholars have offered several explanations, and none is accepted by everyone. They are proposals, not facts. One is that the author's first language, or the language of his Scripture, was Semitic, and that he sometimes thought in Hebrew or Aramaic patterns while writing Greek. Another is that the irregularities are deliberate: for example, that in 1:4 the author keeps a divine title in a fixed form, like a name that does not change its case, perhaps echoing the way the Greek Old Testament renders the divine name in Exodus. A third is that they are lapses, the unpolished Greek of a writer who was not at ease in the language.

The grammar can point to the places where the rule is broken and show that the sentence is still readable. It cannot decide which explanation is right, and a learner should hold the proposals loosely. What you can do is notice the break, read the sentence by its sense, and then check what the regular form would be.

sections.heading: Other habits worth noticing
body: Revelation 21:4 piles up negatives: ὁ θάνατος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι· οὔτε πένθος οὔτε κραυγὴ οὔτε πόνος οὐκ ἔσται ἔτι. In Greek negatives of this kind reinforce each other and do not cancel; the sentence says that none of these things will exist.

The book is also fond of participles used as nouns, such as ὁ νικῶν in 21:7, 'the one who conquers', and of balanced phrases with ἐγώ: Ἐγώ εἰμι τὸ Ἄλφα καὶ τὸ Ὦ in 1:8 and again, without εἰμι, in 21:6.

sections.heading: How to read the passage
body: Read Revelation 1:4–11 twice. The first time, read for sense: a greeting, a doxology, a statement about one who is coming, a title, and the beginning of the vision. The second time, look for the places where the cases do not match, and for each one ask what a regular form would be. The questions test both the ordinary reading and the departures.

misunderstandings: Treating the nominative in 1:4 as the natural case after ἀπό. ἀπό takes the genitive; the nominative here is a recognised exception.
Assuming all of Revelation is irregular. Passages such as 21:1–7 follow ordinary rules of agreement.
Taking one proposed explanation, Semitic influence or deliberate choice, as settled. Scholars still debate them.
Reading the double negatives of 21:4 as cancelling each other. They reinforce one another.

deeper.heading: Solecism or style?
body: Ancient and modern readers have often called these features solecisms, errors against ordinary Greek. Others have argued that a skilled writer could produce them on purpose, as a mark of a sacred register or an allusion to older texts. The text itself offers no comment on the matter, so each reader has to weigh the evidence from the passages and from the rest of the book.

practice.prompt: In ἀπὸ ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν … (words 12–17), which case does the preposition ἀπό normally take, and what case is the article ὁ?

options: Normally the accusative; here the article is dative
Normally the nominative; here the article is genitive
Normally the genitive; here the article is nominative
Normally the dative; here the article is accusative
practice.explain: ἀπό takes the genitive. ὁ is nominative singular masculine, so the phrase after ἀπό is a departure from the ordinary rule.

options: The title is a genitive absolute
The phrase is a vocative of address
The author is keeping a divine title in a fixed form, like a name
ἀπό takes the nominative in all New Testament Greek
check.explain: A fixed-form title is one of the proposals, alongside Semitic influence and the view that the irregularity is a lapse. The other options misdescribe the grammar: ἀπό takes the genitive, the phrase is not in the vocative, and a genitive absolute needs genitives.

check.prompt: What is unusual about ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός (words 4–7) after ἀπὸ Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ?

options: It is dative, though the name is nominative
It is a verb, though the name is a noun
It is nominative, though the name it explains is genitive
It has no article, though the name has one
check.explain: Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ is genitive after ἀπό. A noun in apposition would normally also be genitive; here ὁ μάρτυς ὁ πιστός is nominative singular masculine.

check.prompt: In 1:8, is the case of ὁ ὢν καὶ ὁ ἦν καὶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος (words 11–18) regular?

options: No: it should be accusative as the object of εἰμι
No: it should be genitive after λέγει
Yes: the nominative agrees with ὁ θεός, which is in apposition to the subject
check.explain: λέγει has the nominative subject κύριος, and the title is in apposition to it in the same case. The same title in 1:4, after ἀπό, is the exception.

check.prompt: λεγούσης (word 0) is genitive feminine singular, but the voice it describes, in 1:10, is φωνὴν μεγάλην. What does the mismatch show?

quoted.title: Revelation

Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: φωνήν is the subject of λεγούσης
The participle agrees in gender and number but not in case with φωνήν
The participle agrees in case with φωνήν
check.explain: φωνὴν is accusative, the object of ἤκουσα, and λεγούσης is genitive. A participle describing it would regularly be accusative. The genitive may have been influenced by the nearby σάλπιγγος, but this is one of the proposed explanations.

options: Yes: both are genitive feminine singular
check.explain: ἤκουσα takes the genitive φωνῆς μεγάλης, and λεγούσης matches it. θρόνου is masculine and belongs to the phrase ἐκ τοῦ θρόνου, 'from the throne'.

options: As cancelling each other: some of these will be
As a command that these should not exist
As a question about whether these exist
As reinforcing each other: none of these will be any more
check.explain: In Greek, a further negative strengthens the first. ἔσται is future indicative, third person singular, so the statement is about what will be.

options: A substantive participle: the one who conquers, the subject of κληρονομήσει
check.explain: νικῶν is a present active participle, nominative masculine singular, and with ὁ it makes a noun phrase. κληρονομήσει is the future main verb and ταῦτα its object.

check.prompt: Which noun does κεκοσμημένην (word 18) describe directly, in ὡς νύμφην κεκοσμημένην?

options: νύμφην (word 17): a bride adorned for her husband
check.explain: κεκοσμημένην is a perfect passive participle, accusative feminine singular, matching νύμφην within the comparison. Both νύμφην and the city ἡτοιμασμένην are feminine, which is why the comparison works.

reading.why: Eight verses that hold the best-known departures from ordinary agreement (ἀπὸ ὁ ὤν in 1:4, the nominatives of 1:5, the case of λεγούσης in 1:11), beside regular phrases and the same title in its normal case in 1:8.
